items.stem: Which compound is bonded by electron transfer from a metal to a non-metal?
items.note: Ionic bonding: large electronegativity difference, metal + non-metal (Mg → O). The others are covalent (shared pairs).

items.stem: A covalent bond involves:
items.note: Covalent = shared pair(s); ionic = transferred; metallic = delocalized sea. Three bonding models, three electron behaviours.

items.stem: How many lone pairs does the oxygen atom have in H₂O?
items.note: O has 6 valence electrons: two used in bonds to H, two pairs left over. The two lone pairs are what bend the molecule.

items.stem: VSEPR theory says electron domains arrange themselves to:
choices: Fill the octet at any cost
items.note: Domains (bonding pairs + lone pairs) spread as far apart as possible. Repulsion strength: lone–lone > lone–bond > bond–bond.

items.stem: The shape of the H₂O molecule is:
items.note: 4 electron domains (2 bonds + 2 lone pairs) but the two lone pairs compress the H–O–H angle below the tetrahedral 109.5° to about 104.5°.

items.stem: The shape of and bond angle in NH₃ are:
items.note: 4 domains (3 bonds + 1 lone pair): domain geometry tetrahedral, molecular shape trigonal pyramidal. One lone pair compresses the angle to ~107°.

items.stem: Which molecule has a trigonal planar shape with bond angles of 120°?
items.note: BF₃: 3 bonding domains, no lone pairs → trigonal planar. CO₂ is linear (2 domains); CH₄ tetrahedral (4).

items.stem: CO₂ contains polar C=O bonds, yet the molecule is non-polar because:
choices: Carbon and oxygen have similar electronegativities
The linear geometry cancels the two bond dipoles
Oxygen's lone pairs repel the dipoles
items.note: Symmetry: two equal dipoles pointing opposite directions cancel. Molecular polarity = bond polarity + geometry.

items.stem: The strongest intermolecular force present between HF molecules is:
items.note: H bonded directly to F + F's lone pairs → hydrogen bonding. Note: covalent bonds are INTRA molecular, not between molecules.

items.stem: Which explains why water has an anomalously high boiling point compared with H₂S?
choices: Water has a larger molar mass
items.note: H₂O, NH₃ and HF all boil far higher than their group trends predict — each hydrogen bonds. H₂S only has weaker dipole/London forces.

items.stem: Metals conduct electricity in the solid state because:
choices: Their ions are free to move
They contain delocalized electrons that flow
They have covalent bonds with spare electrons
items.note: Metallic bonding: cation lattice in a sea of delocalized electrons — also explains malleability and high melting points.

items.stem: Graphite conducts electricity, but diamond does not, because graphite has:
items.note: Diamond: every electron in a σ bond (4-coordinated C). Graphite: 3-coordinated C with one delocalized electron per atom between layers — also makes it a good lubricant.

items.stem: Solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity because:
choices: Its ions are held fixed in the lattice
It has no charged particles at all
items.note: Ions exist but cannot move → no conduction. Molten or dissolved NaCl conducts because the ions become mobile.

items.stem: Iodine (I₂) is a solid at room temperature with a low boiling point. This is because:
choices: The I₂ molecules are held together by weak London (dispersion) forces
items.note: Simple molecular substance: melting/boiling overcomes intermolecular forces only, and I₂'s are weak London forces — though larger than for smaller molecules.

items.stem: The fourth N–H bond in the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺, is formed when N supplies both electrons. This bond is called:
items.note: Dative covalent: both electrons from one atom. Once formed it's identical to the other N–H bonds — only the origin differs.

items.stem: Which bond is the shortest and strongest?
items.note: More shared electron density → shorter and stronger: single < double < triple. Order reverses for length and strength.

items.stem: The electron-domain geometry of NH₃ is tetrahedral, but its molecular shape is trigonal pyramidal because:
choices: One domain is a lone pair, which is not counted in the molecular shape
items.note: Domain geometry counts all domains (4); molecular shape counts atom positions only (3 atoms → pyramidal). Distinguish these two terms — examiners do.

items.stem: In ozone, O₃, the two O–O bonds are equal in length and intermediate between a single and double bond. This is explained by:
choices: Resonance / delocalization of the double bond over both positions
Alternating single and double bonds flipping rapidly
A dative bond between the atoms
items.note: Delocalized electrons give each bond a bond order of 1.5 — the same idea as benzene's equal C–C bonds.

items.stem: Which molecule is polar overall?
items.note: CHCl₃: three C–Cl dipoles and one C–H — asymmetric tetrahedron, net dipole. CH₄, CO₂, BF₃ are symmetric → dipoles cancel.

items.stem: Which property belongs to ionic compounds?
choices: Conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water
items.note: Ionic compounds: high melting points, brittle, conduct only when molten/aqueous (ions mobile). Molecular compounds: low mp, non-conducting.

items.stem: For the ammonia molecule, NH₃: predict the electron-domain geometry, the molecular shape and the approximate bond angle, and explain whether the molecule is polar.
markscheme: 4 electron domains (3 bonding + 1 lone pair) → tetrahedral domain geometry (1)
Bond angle ~107° — lone pair–bond pair repulsion compresses the angle below 109.5° (1)
Polar: N–H bonds are polar and the pyramidal shape gives a net dipole towards N (1)
items.tactic: VSEPR answer template: count domains → domain geometry → subtract lone pairs for molecular shape → quote angle → polarity from symmetry. Four steps, four marks.

items.stem: Explain, in terms of structure and bonding, why NaCl has a high melting point (801 °C) while iodine melts at 114 °C and diamond at over 3500 °C.
markscheme: NaCl: giant ionic lattice — melting overcomes strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions → high mp (1)
I₂: simple molecular — only weak London forces between I₂ molecules are overcome; covalent bonds do not break (1)
Diamond: giant covalent network — melting requires breaking strong covalent bonds throughout → extremely high mp (1)
Comparison made: the STRUCTURE (giant vs simple) determines the energy needed, not the bond type alone (1)
items.tactic: Melting-point comparisons: identify the structure, name the forces/bonds overcome on melting, then compare their strengths. Never say 'bonds break' for simple molecules.
